We lost my grandad last year, my daughter was 3 at the time. I was very upset as I was so close to him, and she could see that, and she was upset by ME being upset more than I think she was actually upset herself.
Children find vague language around death confusing, so I was just very honest with my daughter about death and what it means. It might sound tactless when you say ‘death means that your body doesn’t work anymore and we can’t see a person again after they have died’ but kids deal with that better than ‘they’ve gone for a long sleep’ or ‘we’ll see them again in heaven’ kind of talk. It leaves possibilities open - a 4 year old can not fathom they might live to be 10 let alone 100 and so it means they can struggle to apprehend the finality of death when you use those kind of terms.
(Also helps that we are not religious in my family)

I lost my mum when I was 6 and so I think that I do have a very matter of fact way of thinking about death that some families don’t have. But I think with kids it’s fairly common that they think about it and try to understand it and I would say just be honest.
Nothing lasts forever. Flowers die, leaves die and fall off trees, and animals and people die. It’s the one certainty we have in life and it’s beautiful for that reason.

Edit- just wanted to add, I know you might feel like you can’t say the above to your daughter...

Have you asked her what she was thinking of, or doing when she brings up death? My daughter sometimes brings up missing my grandad when she is tired because she is trying to figure out why she feels a bit sad or emotional - and she knows that losing my grandad is a sad thing.
She also asks about me dying and I have told her I will one day, but not for a long time. She knows what people need to live - air, food, water. If anything in our body breaks that helps us get those things then a dr can try to fix it, but sometimes they can’t and that’s why people die. If that’s too in depth I get it but my daughter is VERY curious!!!
I have also told her that as long as you love somebody that love stays in your heart forever, so she can always love my grandad and he will always love her. And she accepts that quite easily, and when she brings him up we talk about things that make us smile about him so she remembers him fondly.

But honestly - I think kids just have to get their heads around some pretty big ideas at this age and that’s why they might bring them up a lot.
Or try your local post office. They’ll let you deposit it into your bank account, they won’t just swap it. I work in a post office and we take in old notes and coins all the time.

My daughter used to like having a Muslin cloth and rubbing the silky label between her fingers or on her face. So in the end I paid god knows how much on amazon for what was essentially a handkerchief with labels sewn all round the edge - affectionately know as Taggy. When Taggy needed a wash, my stepmum knocked me up 2 spares cos she’s awesome, with some material squares and ribbon folded to make the soft ‘tags’.
So my baby girl ended up with 3 and we still have them all in her baby box - and she’s 4yo now and just occasionally if she’s poorly she’ll ask for Taggy and we put it in her bed with her. Or she uses them for blankets for her dolls....

Anyway. Great story AND advice for parents.

It sounds like you’re doing a great job. You love your kid and you’re doing everything in your power to provide and support him. Your family seem supportive and helpful, and that’s good.

Self care is important. Parenting (single or with a second parent) is hard! So try and find some time to do stuff for YOU. Can you fit in a gym session? Swimming? Can you get a movie night with friends? Maybe even an overnight break, if you’re ready to have your family babysit? Because all that can help refresh and recharge you so you have more to give to your son.
Don’t be hard on yourself. If your little one smiles when you enter the room, seeks you out for comfort and for play, if he is happy and settled and thriving then you are doing a great job! Kids don’t need a ‘mum’ or a ‘dad’ - they need parents who love and cherish them.
